title: The Reporter

jokes.text: Here's a good example of a plant you can't eat. See all the spikes? So, two things. One, it's poisonous. And two, it would hurt.
jokes.setup: Jerry is leading a nature hike and points out a dangerous plant
jokes.punchline: His two-point breakdown is redundant — the poisonous part already covers the problem; 'it would hurt' adds nothing but bureaucratic over-explanation
jokes.explanation: A gentle character joke about Jerry's bumbling, overly cautious nature guide persona. The redundancy of listing 'poisonous' and 'it would hurt' as two separate concerns is the joke — a small but effective bit of character comedy establishing Jerry's brand of mild incompetence.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: You can't eat a plant with spikes because it's poisonous.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: It would hurt.

jokes.text: Jerry's in charge of our pre-teen nature hikes. For a while, it was a teenage nature hike, but then we changed it because a girl got pregnant.
jokes.setup: Leslie is enthusiastically describing the Parks Department's many programs
jokes.punchline: The nature hike age was lowered because a teenager got pregnant — delivered as a mundane administrative note
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy and structure. The joke lands because Leslie delivers a genuinely alarming piece of information (a pregnancy resulted from a government nature hike) with total bureaucratic normalcy, as if the obvious fix was simply adjusting the age range. The deadpan understatement is perfectly calibrated — no apology, no acknowledgment of the absurdity. Strong character integration: this is exactly how Leslie Knope processes institutional failure.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We used to do teenage nature hikes, but we switched to pre-teen because the teenage ones kept getting rained out.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Apparently, once you hit puberty, you attract lightning.

jokes.text: Leslie eats the country honeysuckle after being told it smells good, immediately reacting in disgust. Jerry: 'That's bitter. Leslie, you don't eat it.' Leslie: 'Oh! Why did you let me eat that?' Jerry: 'I never told you to eat that.'
jokes.setup: The group has been admiring the honeysuckle's smell for several beats; Leslie and Jerry both sniff approvingly
jokes.punchline: Leslie impulsively eats it; Jerry's 'I never told you to eat that' is technically correct but misses the point entirely
jokes.explanation: A physical comedy bit that works on two levels: Leslie's impulsive stupidity (she's a competent woman who just eats a poisonous plant) and Jerry's technically-not-wrong defense. The extended sniffy appreciation in the preceding beat sets it up well. Jerry's response is a nice miniature of his hapless character.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: You don't eat honeysuckle.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm eating it.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'I'm not an animal. My tongue is swelling up.'
jokes.setup: Jerry says 'the animals know you don't eat the country honeysuckle'
jokes.punchline: Leslie's dignity defense ('I'm not an animal') while simultaneously reporting a medical symptom is absurd self-contradiction
jokes.explanation: The joke works because Leslie prioritizes her dignity ('I'm not an animal') over the medical emergency she immediately describes in the same breath. It's a tight two-beat structure with good economy — the punchline is the juxtaposition of the two halves of the same sentence.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This is all your fault, Jerry!

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: What? I told you not to eat that!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well you should have been more convincing!

jokes.text: After eating poison and reacting with visible distress, Leslie remarks: 'But I have to say, there's a very sweet aftertaste though.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has been in clear distress from eating the poisonous plant; the others are trying to move on
jokes.punchline: Rather than complaining or apologizing, Leslie offers a food review of the toxic berry she just ate
jokes.explanation: This is the best payoff of the nature hike cold open. After a scene of distress and embarrassment, Leslie's instinct is not to apologize or acknowledge the mistake but to offer a tasting note on the poisonous plant. It's perfectly character-integrated: Leslie Knope cannot let a negative experience exist without finding something positive to say about it. The line lands as a sharp button on the scene and reveals her relentless optimism as something absurd and almost pathological.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: You're like a dog that's been hit by a car. You just keep limping along, hopeful but clearly broken.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Did you just compare me to a dog that's been hit by a car?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Yes.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, I've been hit by a car, Jerry. And I'm still here. Still fighting. Still believing in this town.

jokes.text: The press is a weapon and you can use it to kill people or to feed people.
jokes.setup: Leslie is explaining to Ann why getting press coverage is an important strategy
jokes.punchline: Her metaphor breaks down spectacularly — 'kill people or feed people' are not analogous options; it sounds like she's warning Ann about murder
jokes.explanation: Leslie's mangled metaphor ('kill people or feed people') is a reliable source of comedy in Parks and Rec — she speaks with total authority about things that don't quite make sense. The simile starts somewhere reasonable and ends somewhere alarming, which is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The Pawnee Journal is basically the Washington Post of small-town Indiana newspapers. Which means it's nothing like the Washington Post.

jokes.text: Talking head: The Tucker Park Graffiti Removal Project was a great idea that just ran out of steam. We had removed five cartoon penises, not even 10%, when we were shut down due to lack of funding.
jokes.setup: Leslie is using a past project as an example of how press coverage keeps projects alive
jokes.punchline: The specific detail — five cartoon penises, not even 10% — implies there were approximately 50+ cartoon penises in Tucker Park, which was apparently an official government project
jokes.explanation: The math is the joke: 'not even 10%' implies there were at least 50 cartoon penises. The earnest bureaucratic framing ('ran out of steam,' 'lack of funding') applied to a project about removing penis graffiti is the kind of deadpan institutional humor Parks excels at. The specificity of 'cartoon' is a great detail — not just penises, but cartoon penises, which somehow makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We need to treat the press like weapons in an arsenal. Some are sniper rifles - precise, deadly, efficient. Others are howitzers - loud, destructive, but effective at clearing a path. And some are just... regular guns. They shoot bullets.

jokes.text: To this day, I am haunted by those remaining penises. One penis in particular.
jokes.setup: Leslie has just described the failed Tucker Park project ending with funded removal
jokes.punchline: The escalation from 'haunted by those remaining penises' to 'one penis in particular' — delivered with haunted gravitas — implies a deeply specific trauma
jokes.explanation: This is the standout joke of the episode. The two-beat structure is near-perfect: the first beat ('haunted by those remaining penises') is already funny for its mock-gravitas, but the second beat ('one penis in particular') lands with tremendous force because it escalates from general to specific with no explanation. The pause implied between sentences is everything. The audience's imagination fills in what makes that one penis so particularly haunting — and that gap IS the joke. Near-exceptional economy: nine words deliver the maximum possible comedy. Strong character integration: only Leslie Knope would process civic failure as personal trauma at this level of specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So the mural was supposed to be a beautiful representation of our town's history, but apparently the artist interpreted 'founding fathers' very literally, and now we have a giant penis on the side of the Parks Department building.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't see the problem.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, it's a municipal building. We can't have cartoon penises as our public art.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I think it really brings the space together.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I've seen worse things in the parks.

jokes.text: Leslie lists Rule 1 and Rule 2 as both 'stay on message.' Ann asks 'Stay on what?' and Leslie says 'Message. Great.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is giving the team her media rules; Rule 1 is 'stay on message'
jokes.punchline: Rule 2 is also 'stay on message'; when Ann tests her comprehension by asking 'stay on what?' Leslie rewards her with 'Message. Great.' as if she's a good student
jokes.explanation: A nice bit of character comedy: Leslie's obsessive message discipline leads her to literally number 'stay on message' twice as separate rules, and her earnest reward of Ann for the softball answer ('Message. Great.') is perfectly Leslie. Sets up the running gag of characters breaking her media rules immediately.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm still being haunted by that graffiti removal failure. Every night I see it in my dreams.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But now it's worse. I'm being haunted by one penis in particular.

jokes.text: Ann talking head: 'Until now, my only experience with government was trying to get a recycling bin. Wait. Did I ever get it?'
jokes.setup: Ann is describing how impressed she is with Leslie forming a committee so quickly
jokes.punchline: Ann trails off mid-thought, realizing she may never have resolved her own government experience — the recycling bin is still unresolved
jokes.explanation: A well-structured small joke: Ann's confessional drifts into an unresolved memory mid-sentence, implying that even the simplest government requests in Pawnee go nowhere. The self-interruption ('Wait. Did I ever get it?') is a nicely natural-feeling beat.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You can't have more than one styrofoam cup per person per day. And you can't have more than one styrofoam cup per person per day.

jokes.text: Mark: 'What about that thing you did for the middle school newspaper last year?' Leslie: 'Oh. No. I don't count that. That was a smear job.'
jokes.setup: Leslie asks Mark for advice about her first interview, implying she has no media experience
jokes.punchline: She has done a middle school newspaper interview, but dismisses it as a 'smear job' — treating a children's school paper with the outrage of a political scandal
jokes.explanation: The comedy comes entirely from the mismatch in scale: whatever a middle school newspaper wrote about Leslie, she experienced it as a full political betrayal. 'Smear job' is the perfect word choice — it implies coordinated character assassination, not a piece in The Pawnee Elementary Gazette. Strong character integration: Leslie Knope takes local government with the seriousness of a national politician.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I've learned so much working in government, and I feel like I've really made a difference in this community. I've helped with so many initiatives and programs, and I'm really proud of the work we've—wait, did I ever get my recycling bin?

jokes.text: Leslie: 'What do you think her opening gambit is gonna be? What is she gonna ask me first?' Mark: 'How you spell your name.' Leslie: 'Of course. Because of the silent K.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is over-preparing for a routine local newspaper interview, asking Mark to anticipate the reporter's strategy
jokes.punchline: Mark deflates her with the most mundane possible answer; Leslie earnestly agrees because of the 'silent K' in Knope
jokes.explanation: Three-beat joke with good construction: Mark's deflating answer, Leslie's immediate agreement, and the reason she agrees ('Because of the silent K') which is both self-aware and completely earnest. The silent K in Knope is a real thing and Leslie's acceptance of it as a valid concern is endearing and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This diner is where all the political elite gather to discuss matters of great importance.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It has plastic booths, a counter with spinning stools, and a handwritten menu taped to the window.

jokes.text: Leslie has 30 discussion questions prepared for a local newspaper interview. Mark: 'You're insane.'
jokes.setup: Mark asks how many discussion questions Leslie has prepared; she says 'Um... Thirty.'
jokes.punchline: Mark's blunt 'You're insane' lands as the honest assessment the audience is also making
jokes.explanation: The joke is the number (30) and Mark's unvarnished response. Functional and character-consistent. Mark's role as the cynical straight man is well-used here.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: So you have any media experience?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, I was interviewed by the middle school newspaper once.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Oh yeah? What about?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It was a total smear job. They said I was 'overly enthusiastic' and 'didn't understand the concept of recess.'

jokes.text: Talking head — Leslie: 'Mark and I made love once. And it was very intense.'
jokes.setup: We've just watched Leslie and Mark have a pleasant, collegial coffee meeting about media strategy
jokes.punchline: The confessional pivot to their past sexual history, delivered with clinical understatement ('made love,' 'very intense') recontextualizes their entire professional dynamic
jokes.explanation: A masterclass in mockumentary economy. Two sentences, zero context, maximum comedic information. 'Made love' is the perfect euphemism — it's what a person says when they're trying to be dignified about something they clearly have not processed. The pause implied after 'once' and before 'And it was very intense' is doing enormous work. This also retroactively reframes the previous scene, giving rewatch value. One of the tightest jokes in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Her first question is gonna be about the silent K in 'knife.'

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Actually, there is no silent K in 'knife.' The K is completely silent. It's just the word 'nife.' I've checked multiple sources.

jokes.text: Leslie to Shauna: 'I've read everything you've ever written. You did an amazing in-depth article on the raccoon problem here in Pawnee.' Then a raccoon apparently runs through the office: 'Who left the door open? No! No! No!'
jokes.setup: Leslie is flattering Shauna about her raccoon article, calling the raccoons 'nature's bandits'
jokes.punchline: A raccoon immediately infiltrates the Parks Department office, perfectly illustrating that the problem is ongoing and unresolved despite the 'in-depth' coverage
jokes.explanation: Beautifully timed visual gag. The structure is near-perfect: Leslie mentions the raccoon article → raccoon infiltrates the government office → the article clearly solved nothing. The comic irony is that Pawnee's most prestigious journalist wrote an 'in-depth' piece about a problem that is very much still happening, right now, in the Parks Department. The chaos offscreen ('No! No! No!') is funnier than seeing it would be.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: How much did you prepare for this?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I made a list of thirty questions I'm going to ask you.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Of course you did.

jokes.text: Leslie, after the raccoon incident, seamlessly continues: 'And I agree with you. They are nature's bandits.'
jokes.setup: A raccoon just caused chaos in the office.
jokes.punchline: Leslie ignores the chaos and picks up her flattery of Shauna's article as if nothing happened — praising the very creature that just invaded.
jokes.explanation: The pivot from panic back to professional flattery is very Leslie — she prioritizes the interview over the emergency. Combined with joke #14, this is a strong two-beat sequence. The irony of endorsing 'nature's bandits' immediately after one attacked her office adds a nice layer.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Mark and I have been through a lot together. We've seen each other at our worst. I once threw up on his shoes at a Sweetums party, and he never said a word about it. That's friendship.

jokes.text: Shauna: 'Thanks. I was happy with that line.' (about 'nature's bandits')
jokes.setup: Leslie has just repeated Shauna's own phrase back to her ('nature's bandits') while a raccoon runs amok
jokes.punchline: Shauna's self-satisfaction about her own line while raccoon chaos happens around her establishes her as a character of casual self-importance
jokes.explanation: A small character beat establishing Shauna as mildly self-congratulatory. Works as a coda to the raccoon visual gag.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: And this is our storage closet. We keep all our important documents here.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry Gergich
dialogue.line: Oh no! Who left this door open?!

dialogue.speaker: Jerry Gergich
dialogue.line: The raccoons are going to get in! The raccoons are going to get in!

jokes.text: Leslie gives Shauna a tour of a mural called 'The Trial of Chief Wamapo' — Chief Wamapo was 'convicted of crimes against the soldiers' and is depicted 'right before he's killed by a cannonball.' Shauna: 'I'm surprised no one's complained about this.' Leslie: 'Oh, tons of people have. Yeah, we get letters every day.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is giving an enthusiastic tour of the Parks Department murals, describing them with civic pride
jokes.punchline: The mural depicts a Native American chief being executed by soldiers, is apparently extremely controversial ('tons of people' complain daily), but the Parks Department simply... keeps it
jokes.explanation: A layered joke about the inertia of government institutions and Pawnee's specific dark history. The fact that daily complaints produce no action is a sharp institutional satire. Leslie's casually proud delivery ('tons of people have') without any embarrassment is perfect character work — she registers the complaints but has fully normalized them. The detail 'right before he's killed by a cannonball' spoken with the reverence of a docent is particularly strong.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yes! Nature's bandits! That's exactly what they are. They're like little masked criminals, but instead of robbing banks, they're robbing our garbage cans. Which, honestly, is kind of adorable when you think about it.

jokes.text: Ron appears and immediately says 'No comment.' before the reporter has asked him anything. Shauna: 'About what?' Ron: [no response]
jokes.setup: Leslie introduces Ron to Shauna as their boss
jokes.punchline: Ron's 'No comment' preempts any possible question — he has reflexively refused to engage before any engagement is attempted. Shauna's confused 'About what?' lands in his total silence.
jokes.explanation: An exceptional character joke for Ron Swanson. 'No comment' to a question that hasn't been asked is the purest expression of his philosophy: he refuses to participate in government transparency preemptively. The joke is structurally perfect — the setup is the greeting, the punchline is 'No comment,' and the tag is Shauna's genuinely confused 'About what?' which Ron does not dignify with a response. High character integration: this could only be Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This mural depicts the founding of Pawnee. See, there's the river, the native peoples, and then over here is where the settlers brutally murdered them all. It's a beautiful piece of our town's history.

jokes.text: I'm surprised no one's complained about this. / Oh, tons of people have. Yeah, we get letters every day.
jokes.setup: Shauna expresses surprise that the offensive mural hasn't drawn complaints
jokes.punchline: Leslie casually reveals people complain constantly — the city just doesn't care
jokes.explanation: Solid institutional satire. The joke is about bureaucratic indifference — tons of complaints, zero action. Leslie's matter-of-fact delivery of 'we get letters every day' as if this is a normal and acceptable situation is perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Shauna
dialogue.line: This mural is pretty controversial.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yeah, we get complaints about it every single day.

jokes.text: Tom talking head about Ron: 'I play a lot of online Scrabble with my boss, Ron Swanson, and, oh, my God, that guy is the best. He beats me every time. He kills me. He's awesome. I can't beat him. I should just close my account.'
jokes.setup: Tom is describing his relationship with Ron in a confessional
jokes.punchline: Tom is clearly losing on purpose (revealed later) but performs his defeat with such genuine-seeming sycophantic enthusiasm that it reads as character comedy either way
jokes.explanation: Gets a rewatch bonus because the revelation later that Tom is throwing the games retroactively makes this confessional hilarious — he's covering his tracks on camera with this enthusiastic performance of being legitimately beaten. On first watch it's a mild character beat; on rewatch it's a calculated con job.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: No comment.

dialogue.speaker: Shauna
dialogue.line: I haven't asked you anything yet.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I work fast.

jokes.text: Leslie introduces Tom: 'Tom Haverford, boy genius. Smooth like milk chocolate.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is introducing her team to the reporter with characteristic enthusiasm
jokes.punchline: 'Smooth like milk chocolate' is not a professional description — it's the kind of thing a person says about a friend they're trying to set up on a date, not a colleague
jokes.explanation: The absurdity of 'smooth like milk chocolate' as a professional introduction is underscored by Tom's reaction ('That's a weird way to describe me') — which is understated and perfect. Leslie doesn't see anything wrong with it, which is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Tom, you can't spell a three-letter word. You're an idiot.

jokes.text: Tom: 'That's a weird way to describe me.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has just described Tom as 'smooth like milk chocolate'
jokes.punchline: Tom's measured, understated acknowledgment that this is 'a weird way' to describe someone — not objecting strenuously, just noting it
jokes.explanation: A tag to the milk chocolate joke. Tom's understatement ('a weird way') rather than a strong objection is perfectly calibrated — he's mildly confused, not offended. Economical.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ron and I have this beautiful thing where I'm constantly trying to impress him, and I'm constantly failing. It's like a dance. A dance that I'm losing. Every single time. But I keep dancing.

jokes.text: Leslie introduces April: 'April Ludgate, 19. Cool enough to be invited anywhere and chooses to be here.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is doing enthusiastic introductions of her team for the reporter
jokes.punchline: April's introduction is both flattering and damning — she's apparently so cool she could go anywhere, but she's here, in the Parks Department, which is the unflattering part
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels: it's a compliment to April that unintentionally damns the Parks Department ('choosing to be here' is clearly the lesser option), and it captures April's character — too cool to be in local government, inexplicably present anyway.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This is Tom Haverford, our department's... entrepreneur.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm smooth like milk chocolate.

jokes.text: Leslie re-introducing Andy: 'Andy is the citizen who fell in it.' (the pit)
jokes.setup: Leslie has introduced Ann as 'the citizen who brought the pit to our attention'
jokes.punchline: Andy's parallel introduction — 'the citizen who fell in it' — delivered with identical civic pride reduces his role to his accident
jokes.explanation: The parallel structure of Ann's and Andy's introductions ('brought it to our attention' / 'fell in it') is nicely constructed. Leslie's equal enthusiasm for both, treating Andy's accident as a civic contribution, is a good character beat.

jokes.text: Shauna refers to Leslie's group as a 'committee'; Leslie corrects her: 'I'm sorry. It's actually called a subcommittee, not a committee.' — then realizes this is being recorded and backs off.
jokes.setup: The first question in the interview; Shauna mentions 'committee' as a simple word choice
jokes.punchline: Leslie's first instinct under pressure is to correct a trivial semantic distinction on tape, then panic when she realizes it
jokes.explanation: The joke is that Leslie's first instinct under the pressure of a recorded interview is to correct a meaningless bureaucratic distinction — instantly breaking her own 'stay on message' rule about something completely irrelevant. Good irony structure, character-integrated.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This is April Ludgate. She's our new parks department secretary, and she chose to work here, which means she has terrible judgment.

jokes.text: Shauna asks if the group always meets 'here' (the conference room). Leslie panics: 'We meet at a bunch of different places. We don't always meet here. So I didn't quite know how to answer that.'
jokes.setup: Shauna asks a completely benign question about where the committee meets
jokes.punchline: Leslie's self-contradictory, defensive non-answer to a yes/no question suggests deep anxiety about a topic that requires no anxiety
jokes.explanation: A cringe beat illustrating Leslie's media anxiety — she treats 'where do you meet?' like it's a perjury trap. The subsequent 'so I didn't quite know how to answer that' in talking-head mode shows her lack of self-awareness about how badly she handled a non-question.

dialogue.speaker: Reporter
dialogue.line: Can I record this?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yes! Absolutely. I love being recorded. I have a very recordable face. It photographs well from all angles. My voice is also very record-friendly. It's a warm, mellifluous tone that really translates well to audio formats.

jokes.text: Andy: 'I just finished up a gig with my band Three Skin, formerly Four Skin, but our bassist left for personal reasons.'
jokes.setup: Shauna asks Andy to tell the story of the night he fell in the pit
jokes.punchline: The band name 'Three Skin' is revealed to be a diminished version of the original name 'Four Skin' — a foreskin pun delivered with complete innocence by Andy
jokes.explanation: An excellent disguised pun. The foreskin joke is embedded in a completely innocent-sounding band name backstory. 'Three Skin, formerly Four Skin, but our bassist left for personal reasons' — the joke has multiple layers: the pun itself, the implication that losing a bassist cost them a skin (anatomically speaking), and the deadpan 'personal reasons' which doesn't explain anything. Andy delivers it with total sincerity, which is exactly right. High quotability because it works perfectly as a standalone line.

dialogue.speaker: Reporter
dialogue.line: So you're heading up this new committee?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Actually, it's a subcommittee. There's a very important distinction.

jokes.text: Andy explains he fell in the pit because he saw a toaster and thought 'Maybe I should get that.'
jokes.setup: Andy is explaining why he was near the pit at night
jokes.punchline: The motivation for going into a dark pit was retrieving a discarded toaster — the kind of impulsive scavenger logic that leads only to broken legs
jokes.explanation: The toaster detail is a perfectly chosen absurdist beat — not something valuable or even obviously worth retrieving, but just a toaster. 'Maybe I should get that' captures Andy's impulsive, not-very-forward-thinking nature perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So I was in this band called Four Skin, and we were pretty good. We had like a really solid following in Pawnee. But then our drummer got arrested, so we had to change our name to Three Skin.

jokes.text: Shauna: 'Why would you want a toaster that's lying at the bottom of the pit?' Andy: 'I don't know. I was pretty wasted.'
jokes.setup: Shauna asks the reasonable follow-up question about the toaster
jokes.punchline: 'I was pretty wasted' — the revelation that he was drunk, delivered as if this resolves the question rather than raising further questions
jokes.explanation: Classic economy joke. 'I don't know. I was pretty wasted.' is a four-word punchline that perfectly satisfies and escalates simultaneously. Andy treats being drunk as a complete explanation, delivered without shame.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I went into the pit because there was this illogical desire for a random toaster at the bottom of a pit.

jokes.text: Ann: 'Wait. You were drunk?' Andy: 'Oh, yeah. Totally.' Ann: 'You knew that.' Andy: 'I didn't know that, no.' Ann: 'You should've told me, because we gave you anesthesia at the hospital.'
jokes.setup: Andy's drunk confession to the reporter triggers Ann's realization that she administered anesthesia to an already-intoxicated patient
jokes.punchline: Ann is a nurse who gave a blackout-drunk patient anesthesia — a potentially lethal combination — and is only learning this now, on the record, in front of a reporter
jokes.explanation: A satisfying escalation of the drunk revelation. Ann's professional panic is played against Andy's total nonchalance ('Oh, yeah. Totally.'). The medical stakes (anesthesia + alcohol = danger) make Ann's reaction legitimate, which grounds the cringe comedy. Well-structured scene.

dialogue.speaker: Shauna
dialogue.line: Why would you put a toaster in a bathtub?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I was drunk.

jokes.text: Andy: 'I was probably not thinking 'cause I had two broken femurs and I was blackout drunk.'
jokes.setup: Ann is upset that Andy didn't tell her he was drunk before she gave him anesthesia
jokes.punchline: Andy offers 'two broken femurs and blackout drunk' as a reasonable excuse for not fully disclosing his condition — as if these are equivalent mitigating factors
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the equivalence Andy draws: broken bones and blackout drinking are both cited as reasons for impaired communication, with no acknowledgment that being blackout drunk is his own doing. The line has a good rhythm and Andy's guileless delivery makes it land.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You knew I was drunk?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: What? No!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh my God, you knew the whole time?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I didn't know anything!

jokes.text: Andy to Ann: 'Like you're perfect. You're on the pill. You drink all the time. You're allowed to do that.'
jokes.setup: Ann is upset and possibly shaming Andy; he counter-attacks with her personal information
jokes.punchline: Andy reveals Ann's birth control and drinking habits in front of a reporter while ostensibly defending her — 'you're allowed to do that' is not the save he thinks it is
jokes.explanation: Andy's defensive oversharing is both perfectly character-integrated and a brilliant cringe escalation. The 'you're allowed to do that' tag is the key — he genuinely thinks he's being supportive, which makes the disaster complete. The sequence of revelations (birth control, drinking) lands as separate punches, and the fact that it happens in front of a reporter is the cringe cherry on top.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Andy, you could die. You have a serious medical condition.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Ann, I'm not going to die. I'm just going to get blackout drunk.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Stay on message. Thank you so much for bringing that up in front of a reporter.'
jokes.setup: Andy has just disclosed Ann's personal information on the record
jokes.punchline: Leslie's sarcastic callback to her own media rules ('stay on message') while the reporter is present and presumably recording everything
jokes.explanation: A running gag callback that works because Leslie's media rules are being violated in real time. The sarcasm in 'thank you so much for bringing that up' is sharp but expected. Functional payoff on the setup earlier.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Look, I didn't eat the last waffle. Ask Ann, she'll tell you.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Andy, why would I—

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Because she's on birth control, so she's used to keeping track of things!

jokes.text: Leslie to Ann: 'Oh, Ann. You're so sweet and innocent and pretty. The press are like sharks, and you guys just dumped a bucket of chum in the water.'
jokes.setup: Ann tries to calm Leslie down, suggesting they can just go back in and talk about the park
jokes.punchline: Leslie's patronizing sympathy ('sweet and innocent and pretty') pivots into a shark metaphor that is both alarming and accurate
jokes.explanation: The 'sweet and innocent and pretty' setup is warm until the pivot to 'chum in the water' which snaps the tone hard. Leslie's ability to simultaneously compliment and catastrophize is a good character beat. Slightly echoes the earlier 'weapon' metaphor for press.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I've been struggling with my sexuality since I was a kid.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Thanks for sharing that with a reporter, Andy.

jokes.text: Leslie to Mark: 'And it turns out that Ann is on birth-control pills.' Mark: 'Okay.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is summarizing the media disaster to Mark: Andy was drunk when he fell in the pit, AND...
jokes.punchline: Leslie lists Ann's birth control as a media crisis on par with the drunk pit fall; Mark's 'Okay' is a masterwork of not engaging
jokes.explanation: Mark's 'Okay' as a response to birth control pills being listed as a PR crisis is a perfectly dry straight-man reaction. Leslie's total seriousness about both items as equivalent media disasters is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know what? The press is like a shark. It can smell blood in the water from a thousand miles away. And once it does, it circles. And circles. And then it attacks.

jokes.text: Tom asks April: 'Do you think I'm in the top five best-looking Indian guys in Pawnee?'
jokes.setup: Tom approaches April, seemingly wanting a compliment or validation
jokes.punchline: The specificity of 'top five' in 'best-looking Indian guys in Pawnee' — an incredibly niche pool — suggests Tom has thought about this ranking carefully and still isn't certain he makes it
jokes.explanation: The joke is in Tom's narcissism being perfectly calibrated to reality — he doesn't claim top 1 or 2, just a modest 'top five' in an extremely specific demographic bracket. This is Tom Haverford comedy at its purest: confident but grounded vanity. April's immediate 'No' is the perfect button.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We have a crisis on our hands. The interview revealed several major problems: the pothole on Ramsett Street, the crumbling infrastructure at City Hall, and Ann's birth control.

jokes.text: April: 'No.'
jokes.setup: Tom has asked if he's in the top five best-looking Indian guys in Pawnee
jokes.punchline: April's single-word, zero-hesitation rejection is funnier than any elaboration would be
jokes.explanation: One word. Maximum economy. April's deadpan 'No' with no softening or explanation is perfect character comedy — she doesn't explain, doesn't comfort, doesn't hedge. That flat refusal is her entire personality in one syllable.

jokes.text: Tom: 'Who do you think's got me beat? That guy Hashish at City Planning?'
jokes.setup: April has just said Tom is not in the top five
jokes.punchline: Tom has a specific rival named 'Hashish' at City Planning — the name is absurd and the fact that Tom has scoped out his competition within this demographic is a great detail
jokes.explanation: The name 'Hashish' is wonderfully absurd and the fact that Tom has an identified rival — specifically at City Planning — implies he has done real sociological research on this question. Strong character integration: this is exactly how Tom Haverford thinks.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Am I in your top five best-looking guys?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Top ten?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Well, who's ahead of me?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Literally almost everyone.

jokes.text: Ron to Tom: 'Let me tell you something, Tom. You suck at Scrabble. I know. You're destroying me. You're worse than my ex-wife, and she's terrible at Scrabble. And she's a bitch.'
jokes.setup: Ron and Tom are bantering about their online Scrabble competition
jokes.punchline: Ron escalates from Scrabble skill ('worse than my ex-wife') to a personal attack ('she's a bitch') — the latter non-sequitur delivered with the same flat tone as the former
jokes.explanation: Ron's pivot from Scrabble to 'she's a bitch' is structurally excellent — the addendum lands with a thud precisely because it has no logical connection to the sentence it's appended to. This is the first introduction of Tammy Swanson as a character (by description only), and framing her debut as a Scrabble comparison is perfectly Ron. High character integration: Ron's emotional directness about his ex-wife, delivered with zero self-awareness that this is weird to say, is core to the character.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Tom can't play Scrabble. He doesn't have the intellectual capacity. Last week he tried to use the word 'Q' as a standalone tile. When I told him that wasn't allowed, he argued with me for twenty minutes about the rules of a game he's played since childhood. He's an idiot. His mother's an idiot. His father's an idiot. And his ex-wife Wendy is a bitch.

jokes.text: Ron talking-head coda: 'Her name is Tammy Swanson and she's a serious bitch.'
jokes.setup: Ron has just told Tom his ex-wife is a bitch in passing; the confessional follows
jokes.punchline: Ron clarifies — unprompted — with her full name and a graded adjective ('serious') as if this is important documentary information
jokes.explanation: The upgrade from 'bitch' to 'serious bitch' with the addition of her full name — Tammy Swanson — delivered in confessional mode as if filing an official record is a great Ron Swanson joke. It's so matter-of-fact, so Ron. The use of her full name (including his last name, meaning he kept the Swanson name too?) adds a layer. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: She's a bitch.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: A serious bitch.

jokes.text: Shauna arrives at the pit interview — Leslie realizes Shauna is wearing the same dress as yesterday and got a ride from Mark. The talking head: 'She and Mark had sex with each other last night.'
jokes.setup: Leslie narrates Shauna's minor unprofessionalisms (late, same dress) then trails off mid-sentence before cutting to her own talking head
jokes.punchline: Leslie has deduced — correctly — that Shauna and Mark slept together, which she confirms in the talking head with clinical certainty ('I'm not saying... they did it')
jokes.explanation: The investigative chain (late + same dress + Mark's car = sex) is funny because Leslie works it out and presents it as measured analysis in the confessional. The abrupt scene cut mid-sentence also works as a comedic edit beat.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: She wears her lanyard on the outside of her shirt. She microwaves fish in the office kitchen. She refers to herself in the third person. She once told me that she doesn't believe in email. And most damning of all, she's dating Mark Brendanawicz.

jokes.text: At the pit, Leslie melts down when Shauna asks how big the lot is: 'A hundred or something. Give or take 100. I don't know. A hundred what? I don't know, Shauna Malwae-Tweep. I don't know. I don't... I guess I don't know anything.'
jokes.setup: Leslie knows Shauna slept with Mark; the interview is supposed to be a do-over; Shauna asks a simple factual question
jokes.punchline: Leslie completely falls apart over 'how big is the lot?' — escalating to 'I guess I don't know anything' with existential despair
jokes.explanation: A satisfying cringe escalation. 'A hundred or something. Give or take 100.' is a perfect self-undermining answer — it means nothing. The full name invocation ('I don't know, Shauna Malwae-Tweep') signals Leslie's complete loss of composure, and the collapse into 'I guess I don't know anything' is a great absurdist spiral. The escalation from measured to existential is well-paced.

dialogue.speaker: Shauna
dialogue.line: What's the lot size?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I don't know, maybe like... a lot? A regular lot? It's got the lot things on it, you know, dirt and trees and... molecules.

jokes.text: Tom catches April playing Scrabble on Ron's computer: 'I was letting him win, dumbass.' / 'Whatever.' / 'Oh. Come on. Lateral, communal, zonal?'
jokes.setup: Tom has been telling everyone he can't beat Ron at Scrabble; April reveals she got on his computer (password was saved) and played some words
jokes.punchline: Tom's 'I was letting him win, dumbass' immediately exposed as a lie/cover story — and then he's outraged by April's word choices ('Lateral, communal, zonal?') because they're too good and might blow his cover
jokes.explanation: This payoff works well because Tom's confession ('I was letting him win') comes with equal defensiveness toward the person who helped him. His complaint about April's words being too good reveals his strategy: strategic losing requires strategic bad play. The rewatch bonus comes from retroactively understanding Tom's earlier effusive compliments of Ron as a cover story.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I just played 'qi' on a triple word score. That's 47 points. I am dominating this game.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Yeah, about that. Ron and I have a thing where I let him win at games so he doesn't get angry and fire us.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You just ruined six months of work.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, what?

jokes.text: April dropped a 'Z' in a Scrabble word. Tom: 'You dropped a Z in there? April.'
jokes.setup: Tom is reviewing April's illicit Scrabble moves
jokes.punchline: The Z tile in Scrabble is high-value and rare; Tom says April's name as the entire response — equal parts admiration and frustration
jokes.explanation: A small beat — Tom saying April's name as his entire response is economical and shows his conflicted feelings. Light but functional.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I would never hire someone just because they're family. That would be nepotism, and nepotism is wrong.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Also, my sister starts Monday.

jokes.text: April talking head: 'When did you start at the Parks Department? Well, it was a few years ago. My mother got me the job. I was qualified. It's not like it was nepotism. Crap on a stick. Okay, technically, yes, it was nepotism. But... Oh, my God. No, it wasn't. Sorry.'
jokes.setup: Shauna is interviewing April as part of the park story
jokes.punchline: April's on-camera self-contradiction — denying, admitting, then re-denying nepotism in the same breath — culminates in an apology to the camera for her own uncertainty
jokes.explanation: The escalating self-contradiction is well-structured: not nepotism → 'crap on a stick' → technically yes → but no → sorry. 'Crap on a stick' is a great involuntary outburst. April's exhausted 'Sorry' at the end, as if apologizing for her own brain, is a nice button.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The interview went really well. I think we really connected. She asked me about my vision for the Parks Department, and I talked about some of the initiatives I want to implement.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh, and apparently Mark and Shauna have been having sex. I don't know when that started, but good for them, I guess.

jokes.text: April mid-interview: 'It's not you. I just... I'm exhausted. I got, like, zero sleep last night.'
jokes.setup: April is in the middle of a press interview and apologizes abruptly
jokes.punchline: April breaks off her own interview to complain about being tired — not to anyone in particular, just... to the air. It's the anti-professional interview moment after Leslie's intense media prep.
jokes.explanation: A small April character beat — her total indifference to the importance of the interview moment, breaking off to discuss her sleep. Light character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I called it! I knew Mark and Shauna were gonna hook up!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You did call that.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Yeah, you totally did.

jokes.text: Leslie arrives home at Ann's after running away from the pit interview and claims she left because 'I figured I nailed it so why push it, right?'
jokes.setup: Leslie clearly had a breakdown at the pit ('I have to get something from my car') and fled
jokes.punchline: Her revision of events — she left because she 'nailed it,' not because she fell apart — is a perfect self-deception
jokes.explanation: Leslie's revisionist account of her own breakdown is a classic character self-protection joke. Her ability to reframe a complete failure as professional confidence ('I nailed it, why push it') without blinking is Leslie Knope's character in miniature.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: It's like, we got a head and a butt, and just enough blood to run one of them at a time.

jokes.text: Ann: 'She didn't ask about Andy being drunk, did she?' Leslie: 'Oh. No. Just your kind of standard questions.' Ann: 'There was one annoying thing. She and Mark had sex with each other.'
jokes.setup: Ann asks a worried question about the interview; Leslie reassures her it went fine with 'standard questions'
jokes.punchline: The 'one annoying thing' turns out to be Shauna and Mark's sex life — which Leslie pivots to immediately after framing everything as going fine
jokes.explanation: The setup ('standard questions, one annoying thing') and the punchline ('she had sex with Mark') is a well-structured misdirection. The understatement of calling it 'one annoying thing' is Leslie's quintessential inability to prioritize.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So Mark and Shauna, huh? I wonder if they use protection.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Andy, that's not really something you should be wondering about.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm just saying, Mark seems like the type of guy who'd be into like, helmets and knee pads and stuff. You know, for safety.

jokes.text: Group reaction: 'Called it. I called that.' / 'He did, actually. He totally called that.' (Andy about Mark and Shauna)
jokes.setup: Leslie announces that Mark and Shauna had sex
jokes.punchline: Andy immediately claims to have predicted this, and Ann confirms it — the casual acceptance of Mark's behavior as predictable is the joke
jokes.explanation: A light group reaction beat. Andy's instant ownership of the prediction is mildly funny — Ann's confirmation ('He did, actually') makes it a small ensemble comedy moment.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Leslie, I'm just saying, don't take this the wrong way.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: But you're being kind of dorky right now.

jokes.text: Andy: 'He was probably thinking with the head of his wiener instead of the head of his brain.'
jokes.setup: The group is discussing why Mark would sleep with the reporter
jokes.punchline: Andy's anatomical explanation is both vulgar and weirdly accurate; 'the head of his brain' as the contrast phrase is an unintentionally funny way to say 'his brain'
jokes.explanation: 'The head of his brain' as the parallel phrase to 'head of his wiener' is the accidental joke within the joke — Andy has constructed a more elaborate metaphor than he intended. The vulgarity is in character. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Hi, yes, I know I've been acting strange all day. I found an old burrito in the back of my desk drawer and I think it gave me food poisoning.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, I don't know how long it's been there. No, I'm not going to a doctor. I'm going to ride this out with ginger ale and determination.

jokes.text: Andy: 'I bet he didn't use a condom.'
jokes.setup: Ann suggests they focus on making sure Mark didn't say anything to hurt the project; the group agrees
jokes.punchline: Andy volunteers an irrelevant, private sexual speculation in the middle of a business conversation
jokes.explanation: Andy's compulsive oversharing extends to speculating about other people's sexual practices. Short and funny because it's so inappropriate. 'Andy, God!' is the right tag.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm not saying I have food poisoning. I'm saying that burrito was not a Mexican burrito.

dialogue.speaker: Shauna
dialogue.line: What does that mean?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It means it was a burrito made by someone who hates Mexican people.

jokes.text: Leslie to Mark: 'It has come to my attention that you had sex with Ms. Malwae-Tweep. That's personal. It's unethical and it's irresponsible for a public servant to have sex with a member of the press corps. Especially when you have sex with someone who is so skanky.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has come to address the Shauna situation with Mark in his office
jokes.punchline: Leslie's formal 'public servant' ethics complaint segues without pause into a personal insult about Shauna being 'skanky' — revealing the real issue is not ethics but jealousy/judgment
jokes.explanation: The transition from formal bureaucratic language ('press corps,' 'public servant,' 'unethical') to 'so skanky' is the joke — it reveals that Leslie's objection isn't really professional. The earlier confessional (they 'made love once') retroactively makes this funnier. Strong character integration: Leslie would absolutely dress up personal feelings in procedural language.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The odds of this park getting made? I'd say... 100%.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, that's not how odds work.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You're right. 150%.

jokes.text: Mark to Leslie: 'I'm gonna say something. I don't want you to take it the wrong way. But you're being a huge dork.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has been formally lecturing Mark about press ethics while clearly also expressing personal displeasure
jokes.punchline: Mark deflates her entire pomposity with 'you're being a huge dork' — delivered with the gentle solemnity of the setup ('I don't want you to take it the wrong way')
jokes.explanation: The setup ('I don't want you to take it the wrong way') creates the expectation of a serious or sensitive remark; 'huge dork' is the perfect deflation. The word choice of 'dork' rather than something harsher is calibrated exactly right — it's dismissive but affectionate, and it ends the conversation cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Shauna
dialogue.line: One person said the park is 'worse than a dumpster fire.' Another said it's 'worse than that time a sinkhole swallowed a bus.' Someone compared it to 'the asteroid that killed the dinosaurs.' And then this one person just wrote, 'worse than my marriage.'

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, at least the asteroid part was factually accurate.

jokes.text: Leslie reacts to 'huge dork' with visible wounded dignity, then formally: 'Well, I can't allow that kind of behavior from someone serving on my subcommittee.' Mark: 'Well, then I resign from your subcommittee.'
jokes.setup: Mark has just called Leslie a 'huge dork'; she recalibrates and responds professionally
jokes.punchline: Mark's immediate, effortless 'I resign' — delivered as if he'd been waiting for an exit from day one — is a perfect mirror of Leslie's bureaucratic escalation
jokes.explanation: The subcommittee was Leslie's mechanism for bringing Mark in; his instant resignation undercuts all that procedural energy. The comedy is in how little weight 'resigning from the subcommittee' carries versus how much Leslie has invested in it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That doesn't even make sense! A blanket is nothing like a government!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And another thing - you can't just compare taxes to ice cream cones!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's... that's not how logic works! A pothole is not a metaphor for democracy!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, you know what? Fine. A sandwich is exactly like city zoning regulations. You happy now?

jokes.text: Leslie calls Shauna to arrange a do-over: 'I accidentally ate an old burrito.'
jokes.setup: Leslie clearly had an emotional breakdown at the pit due to the Mark/Shauna revelation; she calls to explain
jokes.punchline: Her cover story is 'an old burrito' — food poisoning as the alibi for a jealous emotional breakdown
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'old' burrito is good — Leslie has thought through her lie enough to age the burrito. The pivot from emotional chaos to composed phone-call-lie is also a good character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Who said the park would never happen?

dialogue.speaker: Shauna
dialogue.line: Mark did.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Mark? Mark Brendanawicz?

jokes.text: Shauna: 'Yeah, I guess I'm free. I'm assuming not Mexican.' Leslie: 'Why?' Shauna: 'Because of the burrito.' Leslie: 'Oh! Yeah, well, it wasn't a Mexican burrito.'
jokes.setup: Shauna suggests they have lunch, assuming they'll avoid Mexican food given the 'burrito poisoning'
jokes.punchline: Leslie's clarification that it 'wasn't a Mexican burrito' — instantly trying to protect her lunch options while maintaining a lie
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed three-beat exchange. The punchline ('it wasn't a Mexican burrito') reveals Leslie trying to maintain her lie while simultaneously protecting her right to eat Mexican food at the makeup lunch. The audacity of refining a lie to preserve dining options is perfect Leslie Knope problem-solving.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Those quotes were off the record.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Mark, that's not how journalism works. Once you say something to a reporter, it's on the record.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Well, nobody told me that.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's like... basic journalism 101.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: I went to journalism school for a week.

jokes.text: Shauna reads a series of increasingly absurd quotes about the park from unnamed sources: 'The Sullivan Street pit is always going to be a pit.' / 'Hey, you should write an article on unicorns, because they're more likely to exist than this park.' / 'You should write an article on the Pope getting married...' / 'You should write an article on talking monkeys.' / 'You should write an article about leprechauns.' / 'You should write an article about the sun falling out of the sky.' / This one is just 'No.'
jokes.setup: Shauna asks Leslie what she thinks the odds are of the park getting made, then says others are less optimistic
jokes.punchline: The escalating series of impossible comparisons reaches peak absurdity and then deflates to just 'No' — a single word that is somehow funnier than all the elaborate comparisons
jokes.explanation: This is among the best sequences in the episode. The structure is exceptional: each quote escalates the absurdity (unicorns → Pope's wedding → talking monkeys → leprechauns → sun falling) and Leslie's earnest rejoinders to each make them funnier ('Leprechauns exist.' / 'Why would you write an article about that? That's—'). The clincher is the penultimate quote deflating entirely to just 'No.' — the Beckettian minimalism after all that baroque specificity is perfect comedic punctuation. Leslie's responses also reveal her character: she cannot cede any ground, no matter how ridiculous the comparison.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: I said, 'I'm not interested in talking to you about your problems.' She thought that was romantic because I was being honest.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: And when I told her, 'I don't think you're very smart,' she said it was the most vulnerable thing anyone had ever said to her.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Even when I said, 'You're kind of a disappointment,' she took it as a sign that I cared enough to be critical.

jokes.text: 'This park is never, ever, ever, ever going to happen.' — attributed to Mark Brendanawicz.
jokes.setup: After the parade of anonymous negative quotes, Shauna reads one final devastating quote
jokes.punchline: The quote is attributed — it's Mark, Leslie's own subcommittee member, who said it ('never, ever, ever, ever')
jokes.explanation: The reveal that the most definitive negative quote — four 'evers' — comes from her own subcommittee member is the perfect button on the sequence. It also retroactively explains Leslie's emotional state during the pit interview. The four 'evers' is a nice detail; it implies Mark didn't stop at the usual 'never, ever, ever' but kept going.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: We're not romantically involved. We barely know each other. I mean, I know her name is Shauna, but that's about it. We've never even been on a date.

jokes.text: Mark insists the 'never ever ever ever' quote was 'off the record.' Leslie: 'Did you say it was off the record?' Mark: 'Do you have to say it's off the record?' — a pause — 'Oh, God.'
jokes.setup: Leslie confronts Mark about the quotes Shauna is planning to print
jokes.punchline: Mark genuinely doesn't know that 'off the record' requires you to explicitly say 'off the record' — his question ('do you have to say it?') is sincere, followed by immediate self-horror
jokes.explanation: The comedy of a worldly-seeming person not knowing a basic rule everyone knows. Mark's confident 'do you have to say it?' immediately followed by his own realization ('Oh, God') is a satisfying cringe-escalation beat.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Lexicon is totally a word. It means like, a dictionary or a book of words. It's from Latin.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, no. Lexicon is a Lexus. A Lexus is a fancy car. So lexicon is a fancy book of words.

jokes.text: Mark explains the context: 'You got up because you had to write the article and I said, Come on, stay in bed. That park is never, ever, ever gonna get made.' Shauna: 'Right. And then I came back to bed.' Mark: 'Yeah, but the important part of what I said was Stay in bed.'
jokes.setup: Mark is trying to explain that the quote was taken out of context
jokes.punchline: His argument that 'stay in bed' was the important part (not 'the park will never get made') is both legally/logically absurd and completely sincere
jokes.explanation: The post-coital 'stay in bed' context makes everything weirder and funnier, and Mark's sincere argument that the key takeaway was 'stay in bed' rather than the damning policy statement is wonderful logic-failure comedy. The fact that Shauna matter-of-factly confirms she 'came back to bed' before Mark clarifies is also a good beat.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Your vocabulary is abysmal.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Well, my vocabullairy is just fine, thank you very much.

jokes.text: Shauna: 'You know, I wouldn't say romantically involved.' Mark: 'You know, going forward.'
jokes.setup: Shauna agrees to pull the quotes because they're 'romantically involved'; Mark accepts — then immediately walks it back
jokes.punchline: Mark's 'you know, going forward' is a masterpiece of awkward walk-back — he agrees with Shauna that they're not romantically involved but frames it as a future policy rather than present fact
jokes.explanation: A beautifully compressed cringe moment. The exchange works in three beats: (1) Shauna gets the quotes pulled by invoking 'romantic involvement,' (2) Mark accepts but immediately (3) clarifies 'going forward' they won't be romantic — as if announcing a policy change. The absurdity of 'going forward' implies there was romantic involvement up until this exact moment of renegotiation, and both parties are now on record with this taxonomy. High economy: four words carry enormous comedic and character weight.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Tom is lazy, incompetent, and has no integrity whatsoever.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Which makes him the perfect government employee.

jokes.text: Ron confronts Tom about the Scrabble: 'Tom. Ron, I don't know what to tell you, man. April got on my computer. Password was saved.' / Ron: 'I don't even know what lexicons are. I thought that was a luxury automobile.' / Ron: 'I knew that couldn't have been you. You don't have the vocabulary.' Tom: 'I know.' Ron: 'You can't even spell vocabulary.' Tom: 'Yeah. V-O-G-X...' — trailing off — 'Was that right?' Ron: 'No.'
jokes.setup: Ron has discovered an unusually good Scrabble move was played from Tom's account; Tom blames April
jokes.punchline: Tom's attempt to spell 'vocabulary' — the very word Ron is using to insult him — fails hilariously, confirming Ron's point with live evidence
jokes.explanation: The Scrabble subplot pays off beautifully here. The structure is near-perfect: Ron accuses Tom of lacking vocabulary → Tom confirms it by trying and failing to spell 'vocabulary' in real time → Ron's flat 'No.' closes the loop. The self-fulfilling nature of the joke (the word chosen is the very thing he's alleged to lack) is excellent craft. 'I thought lexicons was a luxury automobile' is a bonus character joke within the sequence — Ron's contempt expressed through pretended ignorance. High rewatch value because the Scrabble con is now fully exposed and the resolution is deeply satisfying.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: It's over.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, what? You slept with her?

jokes.text: Ron talking head: 'I'm not an idiot. I know Tom has been losing to me on purpose. But I like Tom. He doesn't do a lot of work around here. He shows zero initiative. He's not a team player. He's never one to go that extra mile. Tom is exactly what I'm looking for in a government employee.'
jokes.setup: Ron explains his relationship with Tom in a confessional
jokes.punchline: Ron's list of Tom's professional failings — zero work, zero initiative, not a team player — is framed as a positive recommendation because Ron is a libertarian who believes government should do as little as possible
jokes.explanation: This is the single best joke in the episode and one of the finest Ron Swanson jokes of the early series. The structure is a masterpiece of inversion: every quality listed (lazy, no initiative, not a team player) is a damning professional indictment that Ron reverses into a glowing endorsement. The logic is internally consistent — Ron Swanson believes government should do nothing, so a government employee who does nothing is the ideal — which makes it satirically rich, not just a random twist. 'Tom is exactly what I'm looking for in a government employee' lands as a perfect button because it's simultaneously true to his character, a devastating critique of government bureaucracy, and genuinely funny. Near-exceptional character integration: this joke could not exist outside Ron Swanson's worldview.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Mark's like the human equivalent of a participation trophy. Nobody wanted him, but the system made us keep him around.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Well, I'm writing an op-ed piece about media ethics for the Pawnee Journal.' (in response to 'you busy?')
jokes.setup: Mark comes to apologize; Leslie is at her desk
jokes.punchline: Leslie is writing an op-ed about media ethics for the same publication that is about to print her disaster — the circular, self-defeating earnestness is perfectly Leslie
jokes.explanation: The irony of Leslie writing about media ethics for the paper that is simultaneously running an unflattering profile of her is excellent character-integrated comedy. Her inability to process irony is core to who she is.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It says here that you spit on a police officer.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I didn't spit on him, I threw up on him. There's a difference.

jokes.text: Tom interrupts Mark's heartfelt apology to Leslie: 'Whoa! You nailed Malwae-Tweep? Nice.'
jokes.setup: Mark is in the middle of a sincere apology to Leslie about his behavior with the reporter
jokes.punchline: Tom's oblivious, enthusiastic bro-response to the news completely derails the emotional moment
jokes.explanation: 'Nailed Malwae-Tweep? Nice.' is a good Tom character beat — he processes information through the lens of social status and desirability, not through any emotional awareness of the room. The timing, interrupting a sincere apology, is the structure.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: "We'll see." Oh! That's so encouraging! That means they're definitely going to do it!

jokes.text: Mark: 'Yes, but I'm not gonna do it again. It's over.' Tom: 'So she's available.'
jokes.setup: Mark clarifies the Shauna situation is over; he intends this as a moral declaration
jokes.punchline: Tom immediately processes 'it's over' as practical information for himself — 'so she's available' — missing the point entirely
jokes.explanation: A tight two-beat exchange. Tom's instant pivot from Mark's moral statement to personal opportunity is sharp and economical. 'So she's available' is the perfect Tom Haverford line — he's not malicious, just completely self-oriented.

jokes.text: Leslie offers to reinstate Mark: 'Would you like to be reinstated onto our subcommittee?' Mark: 'Absolutely.' Leslie: 'You'll have my answer within the month.'
jokes.setup: Mark has apologized and Leslie is accepting his apology
jokes.punchline: Mark says 'absolutely' to being reinstated — Leslie then says she'll let him know 'within the month' as if this requires deliberation, undermining the warmth of the reconciliation
jokes.explanation: Leslie can't help herself — even when reconciling, she reasserts procedural control with 'you'll have my answer within the month.' It's warm and absurd simultaneously. Strong character integration: this is Leslie refusing to fully surrender leverage even during a moment of goodwill.

jokes.text: After an elaborate ceremonial reinstatement with excessive 'thank you's, Andy in the background: 'Man, that dude has stuck it in some crazy chicks.'
jokes.setup: Leslie and Mark have just completed an emotional, slightly formal reconciliation
jokes.punchline: Andy's low muttered commentary on Mark's sex life immediately deflates the scene's warmth
jokes.explanation: The contrast between the emotional reconciliation scene and Andy's background comment is the joke. 'Crazy chicks' as a category applied to Leslie (given the earlier confession) and Shauna is a low-key mean joke that Andy delivers without any awareness of its implications.

jokes.text: Leslie reads the article: 'Pretty drunk, Ann's on the pill.' Leslie: 'I didn't throw up, I spit up.'
jokes.setup: Leslie reads the Pawnee Journal article; it has printed the interview disasters verbatim
jokes.punchline: Leslie's first objection is not to the characterization of Andy being 'pretty drunk' but to the description of her own physical reaction — and her correction ('I spit up, not threw up') is a distinction without a difference
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the entire media disaster sequence. 'I spit up, not threw up' is Leslie at her most character-integrated: in the face of a damaging article that has printed multiple revelations, her primary concern is precision about her own bodily functions. The distinction she draws (spit vs. threw) is meaningless but completely in character.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'JJ's Diner gets a nice mention.' (reading the article)
jokes.setup: Leslie is reading the article which has printed all her disaster quotes
jokes.punchline: She pauses to note as a positive that JJ's Diner was mentioned — finding a silver lining in the most irrelevant place possible
jokes.explanation: A beautifully compressed Leslie character beat — surrounded by disaster, she registers a positive mention of a diner as a win. Pure Leslie Knope optimism-as-coping-mechanism.

jokes.text: Leslie reads the article's final line: 'She writes, and I quote, We'll see.' Leslie: 'Ends on a hopeful note.'
jokes.setup: The article has been largely negative; Leslie has been reading through its disasters
jokes.punchline: 'We'll see' is at best neutral and mildly skeptical; Leslie's instant reframe of it as 'ends on a hopeful note' is the closing character joke of the episode
jokes.explanation: The perfect closing joke for this episode and for Leslie Knope as a character. 'We'll see' is journalistic skepticism at best, dismissal at worst — and Leslie receives it as a hopeful endorsement. The episode is about her inability to accept defeat or negativity, and this button crystallizes that theme into four words plus three. Exceptional character integration: this joke works ONLY for Leslie Knope, and it perfectly captures the show's warmth-through-absurdism tone. The economy is superb — her response is three words. A strong candidate for the episode's best closing joke.

tmdb_overview: Leslie arranges for a reporter to do a story about her park project, but she and her committee have the worst time staying on topic. She then calls Mark to help her save the story, but it ends up hurting more than helping. Meanwhile, Tom does all he can to suck up to his boss.
insight: Early-season awkwardness: 66 jokes in 23 minutes, but cringe outweighs laughs consistently.
